list.listitem: To diagnose of skin lesion to determine appropriate care, i.e. unknown dermatitis or possible malignant lesion. Punch biopsy is superior to shave biopsy for diagnosis and staging of malignant skin cancers.
Removal of suspected pre-malignant skin lesion, such as an a typical nevus, if margin is adequate.

Equipment needed: skin preparation material (betadine, chlorohexidine), local anesthesia supplies, skin punches (2, 3, 4, 6, 8 mm), forceps, scissors, needleholder, non-absorbable suture material, 2 x 2 gauze pads.

For minor procedures like punch biopsy, clean technique (using non-sterile examination gloves and omitting the sterile drape) is safe, cost-effective, and does not increase the risk of infection compared to sterile technique.
Determine the skin line orientation and appropriate punch size to either biopsy a larger lesion or to remove one completely with a 1- to 2-mm margin.
Place patient in position that best allows access to the lesion for the surgeon and is comfortable for the patient.
Prep skin with betadine or non-iodine based cleanser, if iodine allergic, and drape in a sterile fashion.

Use 1% lidocaine with or without epinephrine as local anesthetic. Remember use epinephrine in skin areas with end arterioles, although its use with digital blocks appears safe. The pain and sting of local anesthesia can be minimized by using small needles, i.e. 30 gauge, injecting slowly, warming the solution, and/or buffering with 8.4% sodium bicarbonate.
Spread skin around lesion perpendicular to skin lines so that the final wound orientation will be parallel with them and minimize scar ().
Apply appropriately sized skin punch with firm, yet gentle pressure and rotate to obtain a full-thickness sample ().
Remove the tissue sample by grasping it with forceps and cutting the base with scissors.

If wound 4 mm or less in diameter, then pressure or aluminum chloride applied with cotton-tipped swap will control hemostasis. Otherwise, close with single interrupted non-absorbable suture for better scar results.
After hemostasis is achieved or the wound is closed, clean off the betadine and blood from the area with a normal saline-soaked gauze pad.

Cover the wound with white petrolatum (Vaseline) and avoid topical antibiotics (e.g., neomycin, bacitracin) as they are associated with a high risk of allergic contact dermatitis and do not reduce infection rates in clean wounds.
Send tissue to pathology in formalin or other special media.
Give discharge instructions including suture removal timings (see ), keeping wound dry for at least 24 hours.

In a well-designed primary care trial, aqueous chlorhexidine was found to be similar to alcohol-based chlorhexidine for skin decontamination before minor skin surgery. Since it is less likely to obscure landmarks, it may be preferable for some clinicians.
Complications of skin punch biopsy are rare.
Bleeding usually resolves with pressure. Incidence is less than 1%.
Infection occurs approximately 3 days after biopsy and is treated by removal of suture, if present and oral antibiotics that cover common skin flora.
Schedule suture removal (see ).
Contact patient with biopsy results and appropriate plan.
Punch biopsy is CPT 11100. This is the code for a single skin biopsy regardless of technique.
1st lesion: Professional fee $100 to $120, facility fee $150 to $175.
Each additional lesion: Professional fee $75 to $85, facility fee $70 to $80.
Patients usually do not need to be off work following punch biopsy unless the wound is in an inconvenient location, i.e. sole of foot, palm, or will get wet.
None.
Standard minor surgery instructions such as keep wound dry for 24 hours, watch for signs of infection, follow-up for biopsy results and suture removal, if appropriate.
None.
